stories.head: Iran war has cost the US military more than $47bn, Pentagon estimate shows
stories.stand: A Central Command estimate given to lawmakers is more than 25% above the $37.5bn figure Pete Hegseth gave in July.
stories.say: A Pentagon estimate puts the US military's cost of the Iran war at more than 47 billion dollars, over a quarter higher than the figure Pete Hegseth gave in July.
body: The war with Iran has cost the US military at least $47.1bn as of mid-October, according to a Central Command estimate given to lawmakers. CBS News and Reuters obtained the figures.
About $29bn is to replace munitions used in the fighting and more than $6bn to replace lost equipment. The estimate does not include repairs to US bases hit by Iranian missiles and drones.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth told lawmakers in July that the cost was about $37.5bn. Reuters said the new figure is more than 25% higher. The Pentagon did not comment.
The war began in February. Donald Trump has suggested he could restart heavy fighting after the midterm elections on 3 November if Iran does not agree a deal.

stories.head: Qatar urges Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz as mediation goes on
stories.stand: Doha says Iran has made positive statements but not acted on them, while Iran's president told Putin the region can solve its own problems.
stories.say: Qatar has urged Iran to show goodwill by ending threats to its neighbours and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, saying messages are still being passed between Tehran and Washington.
body: Qatar's foreign ministry urged Iran on Tuesday to show goodwill by ending threats against regional countries and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, Euronews reported.
Spokesman Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi said Iran had made positive statements but had not yet acted on them. He announced no breakthrough and said messages were still being exchanged with both sides.

He said Qatar and its Gulf neighbours were ready to join a regional security framework. On Monday, Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials held talks in Tehran, and Iranian state media said all 4 countries agreed to keep talking.
In Russia, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian told Vladimir Putin the Middle East was capable of resolving its problems without the US, Al Jazeera reported.

stories.head: Syria-Jordan border reopens as both sides form security committee
stories.stand: The Nassib crossing reopened after Jordanian strikes on suspected Islamic State sites in southern Syria killed at least 7 civilians, Syria says.
stories.say: Jordan's only crossing into Syria has reopened, and the two are forming a joint security committee after Jordanian air strikes killed at least seven civilians in southern Syria.
body: The Nassib crossing, Jordan's only border crossing with Syria, reopened on Wednesday morning, Syria's state news agency said. It had briefly closed after Jordanian air strikes in southern Syria on Monday.
Jordan said it hit Islamic State hideouts after a shooting at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak that killed at least 9 people. It said more than 20 militants were killed.
Syria said at least 7 civilians died in Daraa and Suwayda, including 5 members of one family, 3 of them children. Its foreign ministry called the strikes an unacceptable violation of its airspace.
Jordan's Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi expressed deep regret over civilian deaths. The two countries agreed to form a security committee to investigate the strikes and coordinate against threats.

stories.head: Egyptian court orders closure of independent news site Mada Masr
stories.stand: Editor Lina Attalah was fined 3 million Egyptian pounds for running an unlicensed site; Mada Masr says it has sought a licence since 2018.
stories.say: A court in Cairo has ordered the independent news site Mada Masr to close and fined its editor, Lina Attalah, three million Egyptian pounds for operating without a licence.
body: A misdemeanour court in New Cairo on Tuesday ordered the closure of the independent news site Mada Masr and the confiscation of its equipment, Al Jazeera reported.

Editor-in-chief Lina Attalah was fined 3 million Egyptian pounds, about $53,400, under a 2018 media law on unlicensed websites. The fine was paid and she was released hours after being taken into custody.
Mada Masr said it applied for a licence in 2018 and 2020 without a reply. It said the court refused to let it review the case file or call witnesses.
Amnesty International called the ruling a crushing blow to press freedom. Attalah also faces a retrial on 11 November over a 2024 sentence passed in her absence.

stories.head: Finnish and Norwegian leaders call Putin, drawing criticism from Denmark
stories.stand: Alexander Stubb and Jonas Gahr Støre say Ukraine was consulted; Mette Frederiksen says the call was not coordinated with European allies.
stories.say: Finland's Alexander Stubb and Norway's Jonas Gahr Støre have spoken to Vladimir Putin about ending the war in Ukraine, but Denmark says the call was not coordinated with allies.
body: Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a phone call with Vladimir Putin about ending Russia's war in Ukraine.

They said Ukraine was consulted and that they spoke for their own countries, not for Europe. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said they called for concrete steps to reduce attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the initiative was not coordinated with other European countries. She said she saw no sign that Russia wanted peace and that Europe should speak with one voice.
Sweden's Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also voiced reservations, saying talks with Putin could divide Europe's position, Nordisk Post reported.

stories.head: Oleshky truce widened to protect aid convoys, Melania Trump says
stories.stand: The ceasefire around the Russian-occupied town began on Tuesday and runs until 1 November, with no violations reported on its first day.
stories.say: The truce around Russian-occupied Oleshky has been widened to give aid convoys safe passage, Melania Trump says, and Ukraine reported no violations on its first day.
body: A ceasefire around Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's Kherson region, began at about 03:00 Kyiv time on Tuesday, 2 days earlier than planned.
Melania Trump, who helped broker it, said it now extends beyond the town so humanitarian convoys can pass safely. She said Russia's chief of General Staff, Valery Gerasimov, had confirmed this.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets reported no violations by Tuesday evening. The truce runs until 22:59 Kyiv time on 1 November, Euromaidan Press reported.
No aid had arrived by Tuesday because mines must first be cleared from the road. Oleshky had about 24,000 residents before the war; only a few thousand remain.

stories.head: Waltz says US is expelling Cuban diplomat after shouting match at UN
stories.stand: Mike Waltz and Cuba's foreign minister Bruno Rodríguez clashed on the General Assembly floor during a debate on the US embargo of Cuba.
stories.say: America's UN ambassador Mike Waltz says a Cuban diplomat is being expelled after a shouting match with Cuba's foreign minister during a General Assembly debate on the US embargo.
body: US Ambassador Mike Waltz and Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez had a shouting match on the UN General Assembly floor on Tuesday, during the annual debate on the US embargo of Cuba.
Rodríguez walked to the podium while Waltz was speaking and accused him of lying. Waltz told him to back away and said he would not be intimidated, ABC News and Fox News reported.

Waltz later said Secretary of State Marco Rubio had signed papers expelling a Cuban diplomat, whom he accused of assaulting a member of the US delegation. He said the diplomat would leave within 24 hours, Cuba en Miami reported.
The Assembly was due to vote on Wednesday on a non-binding resolution against the embargo. Last year it passed by 165 votes to 7, with 12 abstentions.

stories.head: US strike on alleged drug boat in eastern Pacific kills 5
stories.stand: Southern Command said the vessel was on known trafficking routes but, as with earlier strikes, did not name those killed or publish evidence.
stories.say: The US military says it killed five people in a strike on an alleged drug-smuggling boat in the eastern Pacific, part of a campaign that has now killed at least 240 people.
body: US Southern Command said a strike on Tuesday killed 5 people aboard a fast boat in the eastern Pacific. It said the vessel was on known drug-trafficking routes and called those killed narco-terrorists.
The military did not name the dead. It has rarely given evidence that targeted boats carried drugs, and relatives of some victims say they were fishermen.

At least 240 people have been killed in the campaign since September 2025, according to tallies cited by Al Jazeera and Fox News. Adam Isacson of WOLA called it the 6th lethal boat strike in 4 months.
Legal experts and rights groups have questioned the legal basis for using military force against suspected traffickers.

stories.head: Cyclone Arnab makes landfall in India's Andhra Pradesh, no deaths reported
stories.stand: The very severe cyclonic storm crossed the coast near Yanam on Wednesday with winds of up to 125 km/h, after evacuations in 2 states.
stories.say: Cyclone Arnab has made landfall on India's south-east coast with winds of up to 125 kilometres an hour, bringing down trees and power lines, but no deaths have been reported.
body: Cyclone Arnab crossed the coast of Andhra Pradesh just south of Yanam early on Wednesday, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said. It is classed as a very severe cyclonic storm.
The IMD reported sustained winds of 115-125 km/h, gusting to 140 km/h. Trees and power lines came down in Kakinada and Visakhapatnam, with power cuts and some flights and trains cancelled.
No deaths had been reported in Andhra Pradesh or Odisha, where tens of thousands of people were moved to safety. Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu thanked officials for working through the night.
The IMD issued a red alert for extremely heavy rain on the coast. Nepal warned of heavy rain, snowstorms and avalanches as the storm moves inland.

stories.head: Xi urges Japan to protect ties in condolence message for Yasuo Fukuda
stories.stand: In rare direct comments on strained relations, China's leader praised the late former prime minister and urged Japan's leaders to honour bilateral agreements.
stories.say: China's Xi Jinping has used a condolence message for former Japanese prime minister Yasuo Fukuda to urge Japan to safeguard the political foundation of relations with Beijing.
body: Chinese President Xi Jinping sent condolences on Tuesday to the family of former Japanese Prime Minister Yasuo Fukuda, who died on 22 October, Xinhua reported.

Xi called Fukuda a politician of integrity and responsibility. He urged Japan's current leaders to safeguard the political foundation of ties and abide by the 4 political documents between the countries.
Fukuda, prime minister in 2007-08, was known for seeking closer ties with China. Reuters described Xi's words as a rare direct reference to the state of relations.
Ties have been strained since Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi suggested in November 2025 that Japan could respond militarily to a Chinese move on Taiwan.

stories.head: At least 60 Christians killed in attacks in Ethiopia's Oromia region
stories.stand: The Ethiopian Orthodox Church says worshippers were killed in 2 districts last week; no group has been identified as responsible.
stories.say: Ethiopia's Orthodox Church says at least sixty Christians were killed in two attacks in the Oromia region last week, and no group has yet been identified as responsible.
body: At least 60 Christians were killed in 2 attacks in Ethiopia's Oromia region last week, the Holy Synod of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church said on Monday, Africanews reported.
It said 14 worshippers were killed in Merti district on 20 October and 46 in Sherka district on 24 October. More than 20 homes were burned and more than 20 people were seriously hurt.

No attackers have been identified. The conflict monitor ACLED said the 24 October attack appeared to be religiously motivated, and the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission said it was monitoring the situation.

stories.head: Two men charged over alleged Iran-directed plot at RAF Fairford
stories.stand: Two 24-year-old Londoners face National Security Act charges; prosecutors say a handler acting for Iran directed vans of petrol to the base.
stories.say: Two 24-year-old Londoners have been charged under the National Security Act over the RAF Fairford incident, with prosecutors alleging a handler acting for Iran directed it.
body: Mohmed Abdulkarim and Nouman Essghir, both 24 and from London, appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday. They face charges under the National Security Act 2023.

Abdulkarim is accused of assisting a foreign intelligence service, which police believe was Iran's. Essghir is accused of entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK, over an alleged reconnaissance trip on 22 August.

Prosecutor Louise Gray told the court a handler known as Ali directed 5 men to drive vans carrying petrol to the base on 27 September. No explosives were found. She said Abdulkarim received payments totalling around £70,000, ITV News reported.
Both men are due at the Old Bailey on 20 November. Iran's embassy in London has denied involvement, CBS News reported.

stories.head: UK and Poland sign Warsaw Defence Plan to build air defence missiles
stories.stand: Wes Streeting signed the plan in Warsaw, the first phase of a UK-Poland defence treaty covering missiles, drones, the Baltic and ammunition.
stories.say: Wes Streeting has signed a defence plan in Warsaw under which Britain and Poland will jointly develop next-generation air defence missiles and drone technology.
body: Defence Secretary Wes Streeting signed the Warsaw Defence Plan with Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz during a visit to Warsaw on Tuesday. It is the first phase of cooperation under the UK-Poland Security and Defence Partnership Treaty.
The Ministry of Defence said the two countries will work together on making and developing the next generation of air defence missiles. The missiles were not named and no value was given.

The plan also covers joint work on drones and counter-drone technology, more defensive naval activity in the Baltic Sea and closer cyber cooperation. BAE Systems and Poland's PGZ will expand large-calibre ammunition production.
Streeting said the plan was designed to deter Russian threats, Anadolu Agency reported.

stories.head: Two men charged under Terrorism Act after suspected firearm found in Derry
stories.stand: PSNI detectives charged men aged 20 and 24 with firearms offences after searches in Derry/Londonderry; both were due in court on Tuesday.
stories.say: Two men aged 20 and 24 have been charged with firearms offences after counter-terrorism searches in Derry, during which police recovered a suspected firearm.
body: Two men aged 20 and 24 have been charged with firearms offences after searches by the PSNI's Terrorism Investigation Unit in Derry/Londonderry, ITV News reported.
Both were arrested under the Terrorism Act during searches that ran from Thursday to Saturday, when a suspected firearm was recovered. A court gave detectives an extra 72 hours to question them.

They are charged with possessing a firearm or ammunition in suspicious circumstances, possessing a firearm with intent to cause fear or violence, and possessing a handgun without a certificate. They were due at Londonderry Magistrates' Court on Tuesday 27 October.
Police said the Public Prosecution Service will review the charges, as is usual.

stories.head: Ex-Met officer Mark Tyrrell found guilty of rape and sexual assaults
stories.stand: A jury at Southwark Crown Court convicted the former protection officer of abusing a vulnerable woman he met during a welfare check.
stories.say: Former Met officer Mark Tyrrell has been found guilty of rape and three sexual assaults on a vulnerable woman he met on a welfare check, and will be sentenced in December.
body: Former Metropolitan Police officer Mark Tyrrell, 57, was found guilty at Southwark Crown Court on Tuesday of 1 count of rape, 3 counts of sexual assault and 1 count of perverting the course of justice.
He was cleared of 13 further sexual offence charges, including another count of rape. He had earlier admitted misconduct in public office and a separate count of perverting the course of justice.

The victim was a vulnerable woman he met through police work during a welfare check. Tyrrell served in the Parliamentary and Diplomatic Protection Command, which Wayne Couzens and David Carrick were also linked to. There is no suggestion his offending was connected to their crimes.
He was remanded in custody and will be sentenced on 16 December. The Met said he resigned in 2023 and is on the police barred list.

stories.head: Parents who murdered 13-week-old son have minimum terms increased
stories.stand: The Court of Appeal raised the minimum terms of a Wallasey couple serving life after the Attorney General referred the sentences as unduly lenient.
stories.say: The Court of Appeal has increased the minimum terms of a Wallasey couple jailed for life for murdering their 13-week-old son, after the Attorney General challenged them.
body: The Court of Appeal on Tuesday increased the minimum terms of Nivalda Santos Pirjani, 35, and Klevi Pirjani, 37, from Seacombe in Wallasey. They are serving life sentences for murdering their 13-week-old son.
Klevi Pirjani's minimum term rose from 19 years to 21 years 6 months. Nivalda Santos Pirjani's rose from 15 years 3 months to 17 years 9 months.

The baby was fatally assaulted on 24 November 2024 and died 5 days later at Alder Hey children's hospital. He had 41 fractures in total. The judge at Liverpool Crown Court could not say which parent inflicted the fatal injuries but found they acted together.
Attorney General Ellie Reeves referred the sentences under the Unduly Lenient Sentence scheme and welcomed the ruling.

stories.head: Supreme Court reserves judgment on Sean Brown murder inquiry appeal
stories.stand: The government asked the court to overturn a ruling that it must hold a public inquiry into the 1997 loyalist murder of the GAA chairman.
stories.say: The Supreme Court will rule later on whether the government must hold a public inquiry into the 1997 loyalist murder of the GAA club chairman Sean Brown.
body: The UK Supreme Court has reserved judgment on the government's appeal against an order to hold a public inquiry into the murder of Sean Brown. The hearing took place in London on Tuesday.
Mr Brown, 61, chairman of Bellaghy Wolfe Tones GAA club, was abducted by loyalist paramilitaries as he locked the club gates in May 1997 and shot dead. No one has been charged.

Belfast's Court of Appeal ruled the failure to hold an inquiry unlawful, in a case brought by his widow, Bridie Brown. James Eadie KC, for the government, argued a Supreme Court ruling in May meant the legacy commission could investigate instead.
Des Fahy KC, for the family, said the murder remained unresolved and uninvestigated. The family believes state agents were involved. Daughter Siobhán Brown said they wanted truth and justice.

stories.head: Leeds drivers who raced before killing mother and daughter jailed
stories.stand: Hardeep Bhachu and Jasskamal Riyat were jailed for a combined 28 years over the 2023 Scott Hall Road crash that killed a woman and her 4-year-old.
stories.say: Two Leeds drivers who were racing when they killed a mother and her four-year-old daughter have been jailed, for 16 and 12 years, at Leeds Crown Court.
body: Two men have been jailed for causing the deaths of a mother and her 4-year-old daughter by dangerous driving while racing in Leeds. They were sentenced at Leeds Crown Court on Monday.
Jasskamal Riyat, 37, was jailed for 16 years and Hardeep Bhachu, 29, for 12 years. Both were banned from driving for 6 years and must pass an extended test.
The woman, 27, and her daughter died at the scene on Scott Hall Road shortly after 8.30am on 16 January 2023. Bhachu lost control of his Audi and hit them, with Riyat following closely in a BMW.
Bhachu admitted 2 counts of causing death by dangerous driving. Riyat denied racing but was convicted after a trial. Judge Ray Singh said a road is not a racetrack, ITV News reported.

body: Heathrow plans to move Delta Air Lines from Terminal 3, which it shares with partner Virgin Atlantic, to Terminal 4 in 2028. The change follows the airport's once-a-decade review of terminal allocations.
Finnair and Japan Airlines will also move from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4, Head for Points reported. China Southern moves to Terminal 5 and LATAM to Terminal 2.
Virgin Atlantic chief executive Corneel Koster said Heathrow had chosen to split the 2 airlines after more than a decade together. Virgin said it would consider all options to challenge the decision.
Heathrow said the aim was to make the best use of limited terminal space and improve the passenger experience. Delta owns 49% of Virgin Atlantic.

stories.say: Winds eased across most of Scotland on Tuesday after gusts of 76 miles an hour shut schools and slowed trains, with forecasters warning dense fog could follow.
body: A Met Office yellow wind warning covering all of Scotland was lifted across much of the country early on Tuesday afternoon, but stayed in place in the north until 6pm. Gusts reached 76mph at Stornoway Airport and 71mph on Tiree.

All schools in the Western Isles were shut, along with 30 primary and 6 secondary schools in the Highlands. Speed restrictions applied on lines including the West Highland and Far North routes, and some ferries were disrupted.
About 7,800 customers were still without power on Tuesday morning after Storms Austen and Boelo, ITV News reported.
High pressure is expected to bring calmer, drier weather. The Met Office said fog could become an increasing hazard as Halloween approaches, and could be dense and slow to clear.

stories.head: More leaseholders to be shielded from cladding repair bills, ministers say
stories.stand: The government set out plans to widen protections as the Remediation of Unsafe Cladding Bill had its second reading, including making manufacturers pay.
stories.say: Ministers plan to widen cladding protections to leaseholders with up to six properties and make product manufacturers help pay to fix unsafe buildings.
body: The government has announced proposals to protect more leaseholders from high bills for fire-safety defects. They were unveiled on Tuesday during the second reading of the Remediation of Unsafe Cladding Bill.

Current protections generally cover people who owned no more than 3 properties on 14 February 2022. Ministers plan to raise that limit to 6. New funding would help residents of collectively owned and enfranchised buildings with internal high-risk defects.

A new scheme would require construction product manufacturers linked to historic unsafe cladding and insulation to contribute to remediation costs. The government says it would have powers to recover the money.

The bill also creates a legal duty to fix unsafe buildings, with criminal penalties and fines of up to £500,000. Building Safety Minister Baroness Blake said the government was going further to protect homeowners.

stories.head: House prices falling in areas covering 35% of UK homes, Zoopla says

stories.say: Zoopla says 35 per cent of UK homes are now in areas where prices have fallen, mostly in London and the South East, though the average price is still up 0.8 per cent.
body: About 35% of UK homes are in postcode areas where prices fell over the past year, up from 12% a year earlier, according to Zoopla data to the end of September.
The falls are concentrated in the south. In London and the South East, 85% of homes are in such areas. Average prices fell 1.0% in London to £523,100.
Across the UK the average price was £273,100, up 0.8%. Prices rose 5.8% in Northern Ireland, 3.2% in the North West, 2.5% in Scotland and 2.0% in Wales. Homes for sale were up 7% on last year.
Zoopla's Richard Donnell said higher mortgage costs had made buyers more selective.

stories.say: Likud leads the count after Tuesday's Israeli election, but exit polls give neither Benjamin Netanyahu's camp nor Gadi Eisenkot's opposition a majority, on a 77.7% turnout.
body: Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud is on course to be the largest party after Israel's general election on Tuesday. But exit polls gave neither main bloc the 61 of 120 Knesset seats needed to govern.
Early exit polls put the 2 blocs roughly level, and projections shifted overnight. With about 28% of votes counted, Likud had 22.2% and Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party 15.4%, Infobae reported.

Turnout was 77.7%, according to the Central Elections Committee. Arab parties were projected to win a record 17 to 19 seats and could hold the balance of power. Both main camps have said they would not rely on them.

Eisenkot said the public had voted against Netanyahu remaining prime minister. Netanyahu called for a strong right-wing government without Arab parties. Official results are due by 4 November, after which President Isaac Herzog will choose who tries to form a government.

body: John Healey delivers his first Budget as chancellor on Wednesday. He has promised short-term relief from living costs and longer-term action to bring energy bills down, within Labour's fiscal rules.
He is expected to cancel January's planned fuel duty rise, keeping it at 52p a litre, PA Media reported. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked him to look at scrapping standing charges on gas bills.

City firms expect fiscal headroom of about £15bn, with about £5bn raised from taxes on bank profits and online retailers, City AM reported. A plan to lift defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030 is expected to wait.

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said Healey should resign if he fudges the defence target. Reform UK's Robert Jenrick called for a much bolder Budget, and the Liberal Democrats urged cuts to energy bills.

Managing director Hugh Marks told Senate estimates on Tuesday that the ABC was considering legal action with Ludo Studio, which owns the rights. He said a cease-and-desist letter should be issued.
The 2024 videos, from Pauline Hanson's Please Explain series, showed Bluey and former Victorian premier Daniel Andrews running each other over in cars, and Bluey being beaten by youths.
Hanson denied the cartoons breached intellectual property. Communications Minister Anika Wells said the ABC was within its rights to be concerned.

stories.head: Mexico's electoral institute names interim head after Taddei resigns
stories.stand: Blanca Yassahara Cruz takes over the INE as auditors examine its contracts following corruption allegations against Guadalupe Taddei.
stories.say: Mexico's National Electoral Institute has named Blanca Yassahara Cruz interim president after Guadalupe Taddei resigned on Monday amid allegations over contracts.
body: The General Council of Mexico's National Electoral Institute, the INE, voted on Tuesday to name councillor Blanca Yassahara Cruz as interim president, Infobae reported. All 9 councillors backed her.
Guadalupe Taddei resigned on Monday after media reports alleged corruption and conflicts of interest. The federal audit office has opened an investigation into INE contracts.

The Chamber of Deputies will now choose a permanent replacement, which could take 4 to 6 weeks. Opposition parties urged that investigations continue, while a Morena representative warned against targeting INE staff without evidence.

body: SK Hynix reported a record third-quarter operating profit of 83.33 trillion won ($62.8bn) on Wednesday. That was up 632% on a year earlier and above the 76.96 trillion won analysts expected, Korea JoongAng Daily reported.

Revenue rose 328% to 104.6 trillion won, the first quarter above 100 trillion won. Net profit of 39.78 trillion won was below forecasts. Demand for high-bandwidth memory used in AI chips drove the rise.
The company plans to return 100 trillion won, about $75bn, to shareholders this year through dividends and share buybacks, the Korea Times reported.
Its shares rose more than 8% in Seoul, and the Kospi index was up 5.84% at 03:00 GMT, Al Jazeera reported.

Chief executive Kelly Ortberg said production of the 737 Max must first stabilise at 47 a month. He does not expect a rate of 52 a month until the second half of 2027, Euronews reported.
The shares fell about 9% on Tuesday, according to Euronews. Boeing delivered 161 commercial aircraft in the quarter and reported a record order backlog of $745bn, AeroTime reported.

body: Mercedes-Benz cut its 2026 forecast on Tuesday, saying core profit should be roughly level with last year's €5.8bn. It had expected growth of at least 15%.

Deliveries in China fell 29% in the first nine months of 2026. Local rivals such as BYD and Xiaomi are taking market share, AFP reported.

stories.stand: The gamma-ray burst hunter, built for a 2-year mission, made its last observation on 20 October and will soon fall back into the atmosphere.
stories.say: NASA has ended the Swift observatory's science mission. Its orbit has sunk below 275 kilometres, and it made its final observation on 20 October after a failed commercial rescue.
body: NASA has ended the science mission of its Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, the agency said in a statement dated 23 October. Swift made its final observation on 20 October.
The spacecraft now orbits less than 275 km above Earth, where atmospheric drag stops its telescopes pointing steadily. NASA expects it to re-enter the atmosphere within a few weeks.

Swift launched on 20 November 2004 and was designed for a 2-year primary mission. NASA says it observed more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and studied more than 1,400 supernovae, with data used in about 7,000 papers.
A $30 million rescue by Arizona firm Katalyst Space Technologies failed after its LINK spacecraft, launched on 3 July 2026, suffered propulsion and reaction wheel problems, Space.com reported.

body: NASA says the 4 crew members of its second year-long Mars simulation will leave their habitat on Saturday 31 October. Coverage of the exit begins at 3pm EDT.
Ross Elder, Matthew Montgomery, Ellen Ellis and James Spicer entered the 1,700 sq ft 3D-printed habitat at Johnson Space Center on 19 October 2025. NASA puts their stay at 378 days.

The Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog, or CHAPEA, simulated communication delays, limited resources and isolation. The crew carried out mock spacewalks, grew plants and maintained the habitat.
NASA says the data will inform food systems, crew time and medical support for future Moon and Mars missions. A 2-week debrief follows, autoevolution reported.

stories.head: Webb finds lava planet TOI-561 b reflects most of its starlight
stories.stand: The rocky world bounces back about 75% of the light hitting it, which researchers say may point to reflective silicate clouds.
stories.say: Webb observations show the lava world TOI-561 b, about 280 light years away, reflects roughly 75% of its starlight, and its dayside is far cooler than predicted.
body: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope say the rocky lava planet TOI-561 b reflects about 75% of the starlight that reaches it, similar to Venus.
The planet is about 280 light years from Earth. Webb watched it for 37 hours, covering nearly 4 orbits of its star.
The dayside was much cooler than expected for bare dark rock. The team suggests silicate clouds may act as a reflective shield, and that a magma ocean may feed its atmosphere.
The project was led by Lisa Dang of the University of Waterloo, with Anjali Piette of the University of Birmingham. The work is published in The Astronomical Journal.

stories.say: SpaceX fired all 33 Raptor engines on its Super Heavy Booster 22 in Texas on Sunday, ahead of Starship Flight 15, when Elon Musk says it will try to catch the upper stage.
body: SpaceX carried out a full-duration static fire of its Super Heavy Booster 22 at Starbase in south Texas on Sunday 25 October, Space.com reported.
All 33 Raptor 3 engines ignited for about 15 seconds. The booster is the first stage for Starship Flight 15, and the Ship 42 upper stage is due to be mated to it later.
Elon Musk has said SpaceX will attempt to catch the ship upper stage with the launch tower for the first time on Flight 15.
SpaceX has not announced a launch date.

stories.head: Astroscale proposes bodyguard spacecraft to protect satellites
stories.stand: The Japanese firm says craft built on its debris-removal technology could guard allied satellites in orbit, but has signed no contracts yet.
stories.say: Astroscale has proposed a fleet of bodyguard spacecraft to shield satellites from orbital attacks, saying one could be ready to launch in under 3 years.
body: Astroscale, a Japanese company with a large UK presence, has proposed a fleet of bodyguard spacecraft to protect satellites from attack, Space.com reported on 27 October.
Alex Godfrey, its head of defence, proposed a pan-European patrol force in which each craft guards 2 or 3 allied satellites. He said one could be ready to launch in under 3 years.
The craft would draw on technology Astroscale developed for debris removal and satellite servicing. The company says it is in discussions across Europe but has no contracts.
Godfrey put the cost at roughly 1% of the value of a military satellite fleet such as the UK's £8.4bn Skynet. The proposal follows close Russian manoeuvres near an ICEYE satellite in October.

stories.head: ESA chief proposes €10bn plan for Europe to launch its own astronauts
stories.stand: Josef Aschbacher wants about €10bn over 10 years for a European crew system, with ministers due to meet in Rome on 15 December.
stories.say: ESA chief Josef Aschbacher has proposed spending about 10 billion euros over 10 years so Europe can launch and return its own astronauts, ahead of a ministers' meeting in Rome.
body: European Space Agency Director General Josef Aschbacher has proposed spending about €10bn over 10 years on a European system to launch and return astronauts, Euronews reported.
Europe has no fully independent crewed system and relies mainly on US capabilities for missions to the International Space Station, which is due to end operations by 2030.
Aschbacher estimates that buying such services from foreign providers would cost about €5bn over the same period. The decision rests with member states.
ESA ministers are due to discuss the plan at a meeting in Rome on 15 December. In September ESA awarded The Exploration Company €760m to develop its Nyx cargo capsule.

stories.head: Lumina simulation models the universe's first 2 billion years
stories.stand: Researchers say it is the largest cosmological radiation-hydrodynamics simulation yet, run on more than 15,000 GPUs on the Frontier supercomputer.
stories.say: Astrophysicists have built Lumina, a simulation of the universe's first 2 billion years that they say is the largest of its kind, run on more than 15,000 GPUs.
body: Researchers at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian have released Lumina, a simulation of the universe's first 2 billion years after the Big Bang.

The centre calls it the largest cosmological radiation-hydrodynamics simulation yet, covering more than 100 times the volume of comparable projects. It ran on more than 15,000 GPUs on Frontier at Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

It is the first such simulation to follow helium reionisation, when radiation stripped electrons from helium atoms. It is meant to help interpret observations from Webb and the Nancy Roman Space Telescope.
La Brújula Verde reported that Lumina produces fewer very massive galaxies than Webb observes. The study, led by Oliver Zier, is published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

stories.head: Gamma-ray burst's engine ran for a record 27 days, study suggests
stories.stand: Researchers say the engine behind GRB 220706A kept firing X-ray flares far longer than any burst seen before; the work is not yet peer-reviewed.
stories.say: Astronomers say the engine behind a gamma-ray burst first seen in July 2022 stayed active for about 27 days, far longer than any previous burst, though the cause is unknown.
body: Astronomers say the central engine of gamma-ray burst GRB 220706A, first detected on 6 July 2022, stayed active for about 27 days, Space.com reported.
Its X-ray emission was still detected about 51 days after the burst as seen from Earth, which corresponds to about 27 days in the explosion's own frame, Techno-Science reported.
The burst was linked to an unusually bright supernova. The researchers do not know what powered it; ideas include a very large star or a magnetar.
Benjamin Gompertz of the University of Birmingham is on the team. The study is a preprint on arXiv and has not been peer-reviewed.

stories.head: Florida team uses twisted-crystal diodes to steer quantum signals
stories.stand: University of Florida engineers say junction-free Josephson diodes can send signals one way, cutting backscattering that degrades qubits.
stories.say: University of Florida engineers have built diodes from a crystal twisted by 1 degree that send quantum signals one way, which they say could make qubits more reliable.
body: Engineers at the University of Florida have developed junction-free Josephson diodes for quantum computing, the university said on 26 October. The work is published in Nature Communications.
The diodes are made from a two-dimensional crystal twisted by 1 degree. Their behaviour is tuned by twist angle and material thickness.

The team says the diodes allow one-way signal transfer, suppressing backscattering that reduces qubit accuracy. The university says it is the first time such diodes have been developed for quantum computing.
The work was led by Yingying Wu. Co-author Han Zhong said higher diode efficiency is not always better for superconducting qubits.

stories.head: Nanotyrannus skeleton 'Jodi' sells for $47.3m at Sotheby's
stories.stand: The 67-million-year-old fossil from Montana far exceeded its pre-sale estimate in New York on Tuesday, going to an anonymous buyer.
stories.say: A Nanotyrannus skeleton named Jodi, found on a Montana ranch in 2019, sold for $47.3 million at Sotheby's in New York on Tuesday, far above its 9 million dollar top estimate.
body: A Nanotyrannus skeleton nicknamed Jodi sold for $47.3m including fees at Sotheby's in New York on Tuesday 27 October. The pre-sale estimate was up to $9m.
The buyer was anonymous, FRNT reported. USA Art News put the hammer price at $40.5m.

The skeleton is about 67 million years old and nearly 20 feet long. It was found in 2019 on land in Montana owned by rancher Jodi Pierson, after whom it is named. Sotheby's says it is one of only 3 known Nanotyrannus skeletons.
Both outlets said the T. rex Gus, sold for $50.1m, remains the more expensive dinosaur. FRNT noted some scientists oppose private sales of such fossils.

stories.head: Up to 2.8 million deep-sea eels gather to spawn off Tasmania
stories.stand: CSIRO scientists say a seamount in Huon Marine Park is the only known spawning site for any deep-sea eel species.
stories.say: Scientists estimate up to 2.8 million basketwork eels gather at Patience Seamount off Tasmania to spawn, the only known spawning site for any deep-sea eel.
body: CSIRO scientists estimate that up to 2.8 million basketwork eels gather at Patience Seamount in Huon Marine Park, off Tasmania, ABC News reported.
CSIRO says it is the only known spawning site for any deep-sea eel species. One female caught had already spawned, and others were close to spawning.
The study, led by Ben Scoulding, used sonar surveys and cameras to tell the eels apart from orange roughy, which gather at the same seamount. It is published in Royal Society Open Science.
Basketwork eels are listed as vulnerable, partly because of bycatch. A new management plan protects the seamount from bottom trawling, ABC News reported.

stories.head: T cells sense tissue stiffness, McGill study finds
stories.stand: Researchers found the physical feel of surrounding tissue influences whether immune T cells become long-lasting resident memory cells.
stories.say: McGill University researchers say immune T cells can sense how stiff the surrounding tissue is, and that this helps decide whether they become long-lasting memory cells.
body: Researchers at McGill University report that T cells can detect how stiff their surrounding tissue is. The study is published in Nature Immunology.
In tests with collagen gels, T cells in stiffer gels were more likely to take on traits of tissue-resident memory cells, which stay in tissues long term.
The study used immune cells from humans and mice. The team has not yet identified the molecular sensor that lets T cells detect physical forces.
The work was led by Judith Mandl of McGill's Department of Physiology, ScienceDaily reported.

stories.head: Congo's Ebola outbreak passes 10,000 confirmed cases
stories.stand: Congo's largest Ebola outbreak has 10,060 confirmed cases and 4,887 deaths, as Europe's disease agency sends experts to Nigeria.
stories.say: Congo's Ebola outbreak passed 10,000 confirmed cases on Tuesday, with 4,887 deaths, and Europe's disease control agency has sent a team of experts to Nigeria.
body: Congo's Ebola outbreak passed 10,000 confirmed cases on Tuesday, according to government data reported by Daily Maverick. The latest situation report counted 10,060 cases and 4,887 deaths.
The outbreak, declared in mid-May, is caused by the rare Bundibugyo species. It is now Congo's deadliest and the second largest on record, after the 2014-2016 West African epidemic.

Kenya has reported 9 cases, and Nigeria became the fourth African country to report a case. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said on Tuesday it had sent a team to Nigeria to help with surveillance and contact tracing.

There is no approved vaccine for Bundibugyo virus, though a trial has begun in Bunia. Several treatment centres and health workers have been attacked, Africanews reported. ECDC rates the risk to people in Europe as very low.

stories.head: Lancet report calls climate change a global health emergency
stories.stand: The Lancet Countdown links nearly 3 million deaths from 2016 to 2023 to climate change and urges a coordinated global response.
stories.say: Heat was linked to a record 710,000 deaths in 2023, the Lancet Countdown says, as its researchers urged that climate change be declared a global health emergency.
body: The 2026 Lancet Countdown report says climate change should be treated as a global health emergency. It was published ahead of the COP31 climate talks in Turkiye.
The report, led by University College London with the World Health Organization, links nearly 3 million deaths from 2016 to 2023 to climate change. Heat was linked to a record 710,000 deaths in 2023.
The authors estimate more than 540,000 heat deaths a year from 2016 to 2023, and attribute 68% of them to human-caused climate change. Fossil fuels still supply about 80% of global energy.
Executive director Marina Romanello said health harms are growing faster than the world's response. The authors want the World Health Organization to create a formal way to recognise the emergency.

stories.head: UK regulator's tests point to needle-free Strep A vaccine
stories.stand: MHRA scientists, working with GSK, found a Strep A vaccine candidate given through the nose or under the tongue triggered immunity in mice.
stories.say: Scientists at the UK medicines regulator say a Strep A vaccine given through the nose or under the tongue produced immunity in mice, a step towards a needle-free jab.
body: Scientists at the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) have tested a needle-free Strep A vaccine candidate with the GSK Vaccines Institute for Global Health. The results appeared in Human Vaccines & Immunotherapeutics.
The candidate was given through the nose or under the tongue. It uses GMMA, tiny bubbles shed by bacteria, to carry a Strep A sugar and boost the immune response.
In mice, it produced immunity in the nose and throat, where infection starts, as well as a wider response. The work is pre-clinical and has not been tested in people.
No Strep A vaccine is licensed. The MHRA estimates over 600 million infections a year worldwide, with complications causing over 500,000 deaths.

stories.head: AI bots made up 76% of responses to UK vape consultation, study finds
stories.stand: University of Edinburgh researchers say bot responses, removed by officials, overwhelmingly opposed limits on disposable vape sales.
stories.say: More than 90,000 responses to a 2023 UK consultation on smoking and vapes were flagged as fake bot submissions, researchers say, nearly all opposing curbs on disposable vapes.
body: Researchers at the University of Edinburgh say 76% of the 118,756 responses to a 2023 UK consultation on smoking and vapes were flagged as fraudulent. The study appeared in Tobacco Control.
The Department of Health and Social Care's bot detection flagged more than 90,000 responses. Almost all of them opposed limits on disposable vape sales.
Once they were removed, 79.6% of valid responses backed the disposable vape plans. The researchers said they could not establish who was behind the campaign.
A department spokesperson said its controls worked effectively and the fake responses were removed. The Tobacco and Vapes Act later became law.

stories.head: CDC deputy director Jennifer Shuford to step down after 4 months
stories.stand: Shuford, the agency's chief medical officer, leaves on 12 November, saying she wants to spend more time with her family.
stories.say: Jennifer Shuford, deputy director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, is stepping down on 12 November after about 4 months at the agency.
body: Jennifer Shuford, deputy director and chief medical officer of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, is resigning. The CDC confirmed the move on Tuesday, and her last day is 12 November.
Shuford, a former Texas state health commissioner, was appointed in April and had been at the agency for about 4 months. She said she was leaving to spend more time with her family.
CDC Director Erica Schwartz thanked her for her leadership. Satish Pillai will serve as acting deputy director and chief medical officer.
Her exit comes as the CDC faces criticism over its measles response, The New York Times reported in an article republished by The Philadelphia Inquirer.

stories.stand: Catherine Hanaway's cease-and-desist letter says Lilly must stop requiring claims data from hospitals seeking discounted medicines.
stories.say: Missouri's attorney general has told Eli Lilly to stop demanding claims data from hospitals before giving them discounted medicines under the federal 340B programme.
body: Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway has sent Eli Lilly a cease-and-desist letter dated 26 October. It orders the drugmaker to stop requiring 340B hospitals to submit claims data for its products.

The federal 340B programme lets eligible hospitals buy medicines at a discount. Hanaway says Lilly cut off University of Missouri Health Care from 340B pricing on 2 July, and warns of action under the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act.
A Lilly spokesman told STAT the data was needed to tackle fraud, waste and abuse in the programme.
Hospitals in Florida and New Hampshire are challenging the policy in federal court, Becker's Hospital Review reported.

stories.head: FDA sets out single-licence route for personalised gene-editing therapies
stories.stand: Draft guidance lets companies file several variants of a gene-editing treatment in one application and add new ones after approval.
stories.say: The US Food and Drug Administration has published draft guidance letting makers of personalised gene-editing treatments cover many versions under a single licence application.
body: The US Food and Drug Administration published draft guidance on Tuesday on individualised gene-editing products for inherited diseases caused by single genes.

Under it, several variants of a treatment targeting one gene can be submitted in a single biologics licence application, and new variants can be added after approval. Currently each variant needs its own application, RAPS reported.
A framework called the Individualized Feature Space sets the allowed limits of variation. New variants inside it can be treated as manufacturing changes rather than new products.
Andrew Byrnes of the FDA's gene therapy division called the current approach infeasible. Rare disease advocates welcomed the move, STAT reported.

stories.head: Artiva drops autoimmune cell therapy after 2 trial deaths
stories.stand: The San Diego biotech is ending work on AlloNK, cutting about 94% of its staff and weighing a sale or liquidation.
stories.say: San Diego biotech Artiva is ending development of its autoimmune cell therapy, citing weak durability of response, after 2 trial participants died following treatment.
body: Artiva Biotherapeutics said on Tuesday it is discontinuing AlloNK, a donor-derived natural killer cell therapy tested with rituximab in rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune diseases.
The company said the durability of response fell short. It also weighed risk against benefit and likely enrolment delays. A planned Phase 3 trial will not start.

2 participants died. One death was judged likely linked to the chemotherapy given before treatment. The other was judged unrelated, though its cause is unknown. The FDA had asked the company to pause dosing.
Artiva is cutting about 94% of its workforce and reviewing options including a merger, asset sale or liquidation. It had about $319.1 million in cash at 30 September.

stories.say: South Australia's health minister says he cannot promise the new Women's and Children's Hospital in Adelaide will be built within its $3.2 billion budget.
body: South Australia's Health Minister Blair Boyer has said he cannot guarantee the new Women's and Children's Hospital in Adelaide will be delivered for $3.2 billion. It is due to be completed in 2031.
A final price from managing contractor Lendlease is expected around the end of 2026 or early 2027. The government will then decide whether to raise the budget.
Treasurer Tom Koutsantonis said he was not ready to give up on the budget and dismissed talk of a $5 billion cost.
The auditor-general's report, tabled on Tuesday, said key project elements remain unresolved. Shadow Treasurer Ben Hood said there was still no builder.

stories.head: US hospitals close children's intensive care units
stories.stand: Units in Montana, Oregon and Missouri shut in the past year, as the number of hospitals with children's wards keeps falling.
stories.say: Hospitals in Montana, Oregon and Missouri have closed paediatric intensive care units in the past year, leaving some families far from specialist care for children.
body: Hospitals in Montana, Oregon and Missouri have closed paediatric intensive care units in the past year, according to KFF Health News, published by CBS News. Overnight children's wings also shut in Illinois and California.
Community Medical Center in Missoula, Montana, closed its unit in October. Its chief executive said it would affect about 25 patients a year. The nearest alternative is about 150 miles away.
A study led by Kenneth Michelson of Lurie Children's Hospital found hospitals with children's inpatient units fell from 1,749 to 1,226 between 2008 and 2022.
St. Vincent Medical Center in Portland, Oregon, closed its unit in November 2025, citing too few patients.

stories.head: 'Mosquito toilet' helps scientists spot viruses in insect waste
stories.stand: A Rutgers University device collects mosquito excreta for genetic testing, finding a complete West Nile virus genome and possibly new viruses.
stories.say: Scientists at Rutgers University have built a 3D-printed 'mosquito toilet' to collect insect waste, and used it to find West Nile virus and possibly new viruses.
body: Researchers at Rutgers University in the United States have developed a 3D-printed device that collects liquid waste from mosquitoes for genetic testing, Euronews reported.
In a test, 50 Culex mosquitoes from a garden in New Jersey were fed sugar water, and their waste was collected over 18 hours.
The team recovered a complete West Nile virus genome, the first known evidence of a Hedwig-like virus in the Americas, and several viruses that may be new to science.
Entomologist Dana Price said there was no reason for alarm, as unknown viruses are not necessarily a threat. The team plans devices that can be used in the field.

stories.head: Trump moves to loosen Biden-era methane rules for oil and gas wells
stories.stand: The EPA proposal would ease standards for small, low-producing wells and scrap the Super Emitter Program, which flagged large methane leaks.
stories.say: The US is moving to ease methane rules on oil and gas wells, with lighter standards for small wells and an end to a programme that tracked big leaks, Donald Trump said in Texas.
body: Donald Trump was due to unveil a plan to loosen Biden-era limits on methane from oil and gas wells at a campaign rally in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday.

The Environmental Protection Agency proposal would set lighter standards for small, low-producing wells and scrap the Super Emitter Program. That programme used approved third-party monitors to flag large methane releases.
The EPA says about 783,000 of more than 990,000 US oil and gas wells, or 79%, are marginal. Administrator Lee Zeldin called the 2024 rule unworkable and says it would cost $18bn.
The plan is not final and will go to public comment for at least 45 days. The Natural Resources Defense Council said it would give a free pass to the industry's worst actors.

stories.head: Greenhouse gas levels hit new records in 2025, UN agency says
stories.stand: Carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide all reached unprecedented concentrations, the World Meteorological Organization said, with a further rise expected in 2026.
stories.say: Carbon dioxide reached 426.8 parts per million in 2025, a record, the World Meteorological Organization said on Tuesday, with methane and nitrous oxide also at new highs.
body: The World Meteorological Organization said on Tuesday that the three main long-lived greenhouse gases all reached record levels in 2025.
Carbon dioxide averaged 426.8 parts per million, about 153% of pre-industrial levels. Methane reached 1,948 parts per billion and nitrous oxide 339.1 parts per billion.

Carbon dioxide rose by 2.8 ppm, less than the record 3.6 ppm jump a year earlier but above the decade average of 2.6 ppm. The agency linked the slowdown to recovering land carbon sinks and fewer fires after El Niño.
WMO scientist Oksana Tarasova said a further increase in 2026 was likely, citing fossil fuel burning and a strong El Niño. The bulletin comes before COP31 in Antalya from 9 to 20 November.

stories.say: Households across the UK can now borrow up to £35,000 at zero or low interest for heat pumps, solar panels and batteries, under a government loan scheme launched on Tuesday.
body: The government launched the Warm Homes Loan Scheme on Tuesday, offering zero- or low-interest loans for home clean energy upgrades across the UK.
Limits are £15,000 for solar panels, £15,000 for batteries, £20,000 for air-to-water heat pumps and £35,000 for ground-source heat pumps. Some terms run up to 30 years.
10 lenders are in the first phase, including Tandem Bank, Secure Trust Bank and HomeServe working with E.ON. The government says rates are up to 5% below lenders' usual products.
Loans can be combined with Boiler Upgrade Scheme grants of up to £9,000. The government says solar, a battery and a heat pump together could cut bills by up to £550 a year.

stories.say: Scientists have named 5 new species of hickorynut mussel from rivers across the US South, including one known from only about 16 kilometres of Mississippi's Big Black River.
body: Researchers have described five new species of hickorynut mussel from rivers in Missouri, Arkansas, Mississippi, Alabama, Louisiana and Texas, Mongabay reported.
The study, in the journal Zootaxa, drew on about 20 years of fieldwork by Shedd Aquarium, Arkansas State University and the US Geological Survey. Several species live in single river basins.
The Tallahatta hickorynut is known from only about 16 km of the Big Black River. Only the Acolapissa hickorynut has been proposed for federal protection, as threatened.
The authors called for state and federal reviews of all 5 species. The USGS says 66% of North America's freshwater mussel species are at risk.

Diesel and petrol both reached a regional average of US$1.41 a litre in October, the year's high. Diesel is up 26% and petrol 18% since February.

body: Switzerland will hold a national vote on 29 November on a citizens' initiative to restrict noisy fireworks, Euronews reported.
The proposal would curb private sales of loud fireworks while keeping quieter ones such as sparklers legal. It gathered over 137,000 signatures, above the 100,000 needed.
Backers including animal welfare and environmental groups cite noise, air pollution, litter and fire risk. Federal data show fireworks produce 2-3% of the country's annual particulate emissions.
The Swiss People's Party and the Centre Party oppose it. A poll by broadcaster SBC released on 23 October found 69% support.

stories.stand: A declassified version of the March opinion was due by 13 September; the senators want an explanation by 6 November.
body: Democratic senators Ron Wyden and Adam Schiff have written to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Attorney General Todd Blanche, demanding the release of a secret court opinion.
By law, a declassified version of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court ruling was due within 180 days, by 13 September. It has not been published.

The opinion reportedly criticised search filters that let analysts pull Americans' messages from intercepted data without required approvals. The court still approved another year of Section 702 surveillance.

body: Sweden's Government Offices, which serve the prime minister and ministries, blocked browser access to OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude on work computers from Monday 26 October.

body: Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post on Tuesday that his administration would officially ban the term AI, or artificial intelligence, in relevant documents, Newsweek reported.
He called AI a very bad and inaccurate name and said SI, for Super Intelligence, would soon be widely used.

A White House spokesperson said the name reinforces the administration's focus on American innovation.

body: Google DeepMind released Genie 4, its latest world model, as a research preview on 27 October. It generates interactive, realistic scenes that users explore in real time.
Unlike earlier versions, it produces matching audio, including music, background sound and dialogue. Users can change the weather or camera angle, or add people and objects, mid-simulation.
TechCrunch reported that scenes stay consistent for up to 2 minutes, double Genie 3's limit. Google says details can still drift in longer sessions.
Access is limited to trusted testers. It will reach Google AI Ultra subscribers through Project Genie, and some developer partners. Generated video and audio carry SynthID watermarks.

body: Google has opened applications for its Registered App Stores programme, AndroidPure reported on 28 October. From 1 December, approved third-party stores can install and update apps with one tap.

body: The Dutch public broadcaster NPO announced on Tuesday that the Netherlands will not take part in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest.

NPO had said in September that it would return carefully after talks with the European Broadcasting Union. Its executive chair, Jet de Ranitz, said it was now too early to participate and cited sensitivities around current themes.
Media director Jurre Bosman said Israel's participation had caused discussion and division in Dutch society. NPO will still broadcast the contest.
Eurovision 2027 is due to be held in Burgas, Bulgaria, with the final on 15 May. Ireland and Czechia have also said they will not take part, and Spain's broadcaster has backed a boycott.

body: Researchers have identified silk residues on 101 objects from the sacrificial pits at Sanxingdui in Sichuan, China, Arkeonews reported. The study appeared in the journal Antiquity on 26 October.
The objects include 94 bronzes, as well as gold foil, jade and ivory. A large bronze mask from Pit K3 has silk traces around its right eyebrow and eye.

The finds date to the late Shang period, about 1300 to 1046 BC. The study does not establish where the silk was made.

stories.say: Bagan's temple plain in Myanmar has hosted its first official sky lantern festival, with about 1,000 lanterns released each evening during the Thadingyut festival of lights.
body: Bagan in Myanmar held its first official sky lantern festival over its ancient temples from 25 to 27 October, Africanews reported.
It coincided with Thadingyut, the festival of lights that marks the end of the 3-month Buddhist rainy-season retreat. About 1,000 lanterns were released each evening.
Africanews said the event was organised by the military authorities' tourism department to attract visitors. Bagan is a Unesco World Heritage site.

stories.head: Fourth-tier Fleetwood knock Arsenal out of the Carabao Cup on penalties
stories.say: League Two Fleetwood beat Arsenal 5-3 on penalties after a 1-1 draw in the Carabao Cup fourth round on Tuesday, with Max Dowman sent off late on.
stories.stand: Fleetwood scored all 5 of their spot-kicks after Viktor Gyokeres cancelled out Aaron Loupalo-Bi's opener.
body: Fleetwood Town, who were 18th in League Two, knocked Arsenal out of the Carabao Cup fourth round on Tuesday night. The tie ended 1-1 and Fleetwood won the shootout 5-3.
Aaron Loupalo-Bi gave Fleetwood the lead in the 21st minute. Viktor Gyokeres equalised early in the second half. Arsenal's 16-year-old Max Dowman was sent off in the 86th minute for violent conduct.
Bruno Guimaraes missed Arsenal's 4th penalty, and Fleetwood scored all 5 of theirs. Play had earlier been stopped for nearly 8 minutes after a drone was seen over the stadium, ABC News reported.
Mikel Arteta, who said he made 9 changes, called it a very sad day but said he could not fault his players' attitude.

stories.head: Manchester United keep Carrick in charge for Chelsea trip
stories.say: Manchester United are sticking with Michael Carrick for now, and he is expected to lead the side at Chelsea on Saturday despite an 8-game run without a win.
stories.stand: Talks involving chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox ended with no change, though Carrick's long-term future remains unclear.
body: Michael Carrick will stay on as Manchester United head coach for now and is expected to take charge at Chelsea on Saturday, the Manchester Evening News and ESPN reported.
Chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox held talks on Monday. The Manchester Evening News said co-owners the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe were also involved.
United have gone 8 games without a win. ESPN said they are 16th, 1 point above the relegation zone, after a 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth.
Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann are seen as front-runners if the club does make a change, both outlets reported.

stories.head: Barcelona fined €602 over approach for Atlético's Julián Álvarez
stories.say: Spain's football federation has fined Barcelona 602 euros, the maximum for the offence, after Atlético Madrid complained about an approach for Julián Álvarez.
stories.stand: The federation applied a rule requiring clubs to notify a player's current club in writing before opening talks.
body: The Royal Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) has fined Barcelona €602 over their contact with Atlético Madrid striker Julián Álvarez, El Debate and Barca Universal reported, citing Mundo Deportivo.
The fine was issued under Article 133 of the federation's rules. It requires a club to notify a player's current club in writing before starting talks. €602 is the maximum penalty for the offence.

Atlético filed the complaint. Barca Universal said FIFA could not open a case because it lacked jurisdiction. El Debate noted a similar 2019 case involving Antoine Griezmann, settled with a €300 payment.

stories.say: Kylian Mbappé apologised on Tuesday for an ill-judged remark about a Mao Zedong meme, after 3 Chinese firms dropped him and state media said La Liga broadcasts would stop.
stories.stand: The Real Madrid forward said he was sincerely sorry, while La Liga said it deeply regrets the offence caused.
body: Kylian Mbappé apologised on Tuesday evening for comments about a meme that put his face on Mao Zedong's body. He called his remark ill-judged and apologised to everyone his words had upset, ABC News and Fox News reported.
The clip appeared to come from a backstage interview with the French talk show The Bridge. ABC News said it could not verify the video.
Dongpeng Beverage Group, Mengniu and Milkground ended their partnerships with him, according to ABC News. Chinese state media said broadcasts of La Liga matches would be suspended.
La Liga said it deeply regrets the offence and that the comments were made in a personal capacity.

stories.head: Starc takes 6-72 as South Africa make 329 in deciding Test
stories.say: Mitchell Starc took 6 for 72 on day 1 of the deciding Test at Newlands as Australia bowled South Africa out for 329, after the hosts had been 158 without loss at lunch.
stories.stand: Debutant Marques Ackerman made 95, but a late burst from Starc with the second new ball swung the opening day Australia's way.
body: Australia bowled South Africa out for 329 on the first day of the third and deciding Test in Cape Town on Tuesday. The series is level at 1-1, LiveScore reported.
South Africa were 158 without loss at lunch. Marques Ackerman made 95 on his Test debut and Aiden Markram scored 78.
Mitchell Starc took 6-72, his 20th Test five-wicket haul, with a burst of wickets after the second new ball. Nathan Lyon took 2-71.
Captain Pat Cummins finished wicketless with 0-73. Steve Smith was ruled out after his neck injury did not recover, ABC News said.

stories.stand: Dilshan Madushanka took a career-best 5-34 and Kamindu Mendis made 62 not out, leaving England's last game against Sri Lanka a dead rubber.
body: Sri Lanka beat Pakistan by 8 wickets in the one-day tri-series at the Gaddafi Stadium in Lahore on Tuesday. The result knocked England out of contention for the final.
Pakistan were bowled out for 110. Dilshan Madushanka took a career-best 5-34. Kamindu Mendis then made 62 not out off 60 balls as Sri Lanka finished on 114-2 in 18.1 overs.
Pakistan had already qualified for the final. England needed a Pakistan win to stay alive, and their match against Sri Lanka on Thursday is now a dead rubber.

stories.stand: His 35-ball hundred powered a chase that put India 3-0 up in the five-match T20 series.

stories.head: FIA proposal points F1 towards simpler, cheaper V8 hybrids
stories.say: Formula 1 could switch to cheaper 2-litre-plus V8 turbo-hybrid engines in 2030 or 2031 under an FIA document sent to manufacturers, with the engine cost cap halved.
stories.stand: The plan cuts energy recovery from 350kW to 200kW, keeps fully sustainable fuel and aims for approval by the World Motor Sport Council in December.
body: The FIA has sent F1's 6 power unit manufacturers a document proposing simpler, cheaper V8 turbo-hybrid engines from 2030 or 2031, GPFans reported, citing BBC Sport.
The plan calls for a V8 of 2.0 to 2.3 litres, with about 900 horsepower mostly from the combustion engine. Energy recovery would drop from 350kW to 200kW.
The proposal would halve the current $190 million annual engine budget cap and keep fully sustainable fuel. It also targets cutting 80kg from car weight.
GPFans said the basic architecture is broadly acceptable to all manufacturers. The aim is to put a final proposal to the World Motor Sport Council in December.

stories.head: Wawrinka's career ends with first-round defeat in Basel
stories.say: Stan Wawrinka, winner of 3 Grand Slam titles, has played his final match, losing 7-5, 7-6 to Jiri Lehecka at his home tournament in Basel at the age of 41.
stories.stand: The Swiss won the Australian Open, French Open and US Open, and helped Switzerland win the Davis Cup in 2014.
body: Stan Wawrinka ended his playing career at the Swiss Indoors in Basel, losing 7-5, 7-6(2) in the first round to 8th seed Jiri Lehecka, ABC News reported.
The 41-year-old won 3 Grand Slam titles: the 2014 Australian Open, the 2015 French Open and the 2016 US Open.
He won Olympic doubles gold with Roger Federer in 2008 and helped Switzerland win the Davis Cup in 2014. He reached No 3 in the world and won 16 tour-level titles.
He had announced in December that 2026 would be his final season.

stories.stand: Fly-half Fin Smith has until Wednesday to prove his fitness before England face Australia on 8 November.
body: Bath flanker Guy Pepper will miss England's Tests against Australia, Japan and New Zealand with an ankle injury suffered against Gloucester, RugbyPass and The Ruck reported.
Bristol centre Benhard Janse van Rensburg has been stood down from full rugby indefinitely after 2 concussions in 3 games. Steve Borthwick said a specialist advised weeks of non-contact work.
Fin Smith has a calf strain and was given until Wednesday to recover. RugbyPass said George Ford or Marcus Smith would start at fly-half if he is ruled out.

stories.head: Kurtley Beale, 37, recalled by Wallabies for UK tour
stories.say: Kurtley Beale, 37 and with 95 Test caps, has been recalled by Australia for their tour to face England, Scotland and Wales, replacing the unavailable Hunter Paisami.
stories.stand: Coach Les Kiss also added James Ramm and Kalani Thomas to the squad, which leaves for the UK on Saturday.
body: Kurtley Beale has been recalled to the Wallabies squad at 37, Australian Associated Press and RugbyPass reported. He has 95 Test caps and last played for Australia against Wales in Cardiff in 2021.
He replaces midfielder Hunter Paisami, who is unavailable for personal reasons. Uncapped winger James Ramm and scrum-half Kalani Thomas were also added.
Les Kiss said Beale would mainly cover inside centre. Australia play England, Scotland and Wales, then the Nations Championship finals from 21 to 23 November.
